doc.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

title: Starting his own band in the 1970s after tempo complaints
summary: He started a band to hear his charts as conceived; Woody Herman once advised it after Holman griped about a tempo.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. Next day. Well that’s partly why I started my band, in the 70s. Because for years I’d been writing charts and either taking them down to a rehearsal or putting them in the mail and sending them somewhere, and never seeing the music again and not hearing it until I heard this band’s particular interpretation of what I’d written. And a lot of times it wasn’t exactly what I had in mind. But the simplest thing was to start my own band, which Woody Herman told me to do one time. I griped at him about a tempo and he said, “well what we tell the arrangers that are unhappy, we tell them to start their own band.” So that’s what I did.

That must be an interesting situation. I mean by the time you finish a chart, you must know exactly, I mean you have your own conception of the tempo and the whole thing. Then to hand it over and the guy counts it off at a different tempo. And you’re hoping that it works I guess, at that speed.

Well usually I don’t have any idea that’s what they’re doing until I hear it on a record or on a broadcast or hear the band in person. But it’s very hard to get your conception of a piece of music across to somebody else without actually going there and doing it yourself. Because he reads it, he looks at a metronome mark, and even if he gets the mark right, the feeling might not be the same.
